answer: A habitat survey exchange buys one accepted report per river grid cell each day, covering details such as a violet patch or a hollow tree. Payment is keyed to that cell and day, not the submitting account; an atomic claim record prevents two aliases from collecting twice, and signup earns nothing. Reports need fresh sensor evidence checked against independent spot samples. To earn more, an attacker must survey additional cells or forge evidence and risk rejection, rather than create names. This requires trustworthy location checks and a way to resolve disputed claims.
